title: Kestrelmoor Freight Cooperative — dispatch modernization
source_material:
FICTIONAL — written for the CCR proof of concept. Kestrelmoor Freight Cooperative is not a real organisation and none of this happened.

DELIVERY LEAD'S SUMMARY (project close-out, March)

Kestrelmoor Freight Cooperative is a member-owned freight network in the US Midwest: about 1,400 independent carriers who share one dispatch desk, one load board and one back office. Members haul mostly agricultural and building-materials freight across nine states.

When we started, dispatch still ran on a 1990s IBM i system with roughly 310,000 lines of RPG. Loads came in by phone and email, a dispatcher keyed them in, then phoned around member carriers until someone took the load. Median time from a load arriving to a carrier accepting it was 47 minutes. Nobody could see where trucks were until drivers called in, so a lot of trucks ran home empty. Two of the four people who understood the RPG code were due to retire within eighteen months, which is what finally got the board to fund the work.

We ran it as an AI-enabled modernization in three streams over nine months:
- AI-assisted code conversion of the RPG estate to Java services. Our conversion agents produced first drafts of the business rules and engineers reviewed every one. About 60% of modules converted with minor edits; the rest were rewritten by hand.
- A load-matching service that ranks available member carriers for each new load by location, equipment and hours of service, and offers the load to the top matches in the app.
- A carrier mobile app (iOS and Android) where drivers see offered loads, accept with one tap, and share location while on a load.
- A small data platform pulling telematics, load and settlement data into one place, with a dispatch dashboard on top.
- CI/CD pipelines and automated regression tests built from the old system's own transaction history, so every converted rule was checked against real past loads.
- Change management and training for the dispatch desk: twelve dispatchers moved from phoning carriers to supervising matches.

MEASURED RESULTS (from Kestrelmoor's own reporting, six months after go-live)
- Median load-to-acceptance time fell from 47 minutes to 12 minutes, a 74% reduction. Source: dispatch system timestamps, all loads, October to March compared with the same months a year earlier.
- Empty miles fell 18% across the member fleet. Source: telematics, Q4 compared with the previous Q4.
- 82% of member carriers were active in the app within six months of launch.
- The legacy IBM i system was switched off in month nine, on schedule.

NOT YET MEASURED
- Kestrelmoor's finance team projects roughly 35% lower annual maintenance cost once the old hosting contract ends. This is a projection, not a result. If it is used at all it must be called anticipated.

CLIENT INTERVIEW — Dana Okafor, Chief Operating Officer (notes, lightly edited)
"Our dispatchers used to spend the whole day on the phone. Now they spend it on the loads that actually need a person — the odd equipment, the weather reroutes."
"The thing I didn't expect was the drivers. They like seeing the offers themselves. We had carriers who'd stopped taking our loads come back because of the app."
"Converting the old code was the part everyone was scared of. Having the new system replay a year of real loads before we switched was what let the board sleep."

NOT FOR PUBLICATION
- Contract value and day rates are confidential to Kestrelmoor.
- There was a two-day outage of the load board in month four caused by a carrier-data import. Resolved; do not mention externally.
- Kestrelmoor has not approved use of its logo.
